claims.text: Engineered interfaces in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings impede dislocation climb and migration under sustained thermal and mechanical loading.
The multilayer coating consists of alternating high-entropy-alloy layers with coherent or semi-coherent interfaces.
Each layer retains distinct lattice parameters and defect structures.
A controlled comparison of multilayer and monolithic coatings of equivalent overall composition can isolate the effect of engineered interfaces on creep.
Diffusion-controlled creep dominated by dislocation climb applies at approximately 500–700 °C under the proposed stresses.
Lattice mismatch and interfacial energy barriers inhibit dislocation motion at engineered interlayer interfaces.
Stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion can dominate high-temperature creep in a high-entropy alloy.
Multilayer interfaces pin dislocations and elevate the effective activation energy for dislocation movement.
Interfacial pinning reduces creep rate relative to a compositionally equivalent monolithic coating.
Multilayer coatings will accumulate significantly less time-dependent strain or exhibit lower creep rates than monolithic coatings.
Creep-tested multilayer coatings will show dislocation pile-ups near interfaces.
Creep-tested multilayer coatings will show less dynamic recrystallization near interfaces than monolithic controls.
The proposed interface-controlled mechanism is applicable only where diffusion-assisted creep and dislocation climb are the primary deformation processes.
The proposed mechanism requires interfaces to remain stable without significant interdiffusion or degradation.
The magnitude of creep-rate reduction depends on interface quality and stability.
Dynamic precipitation may interact with the interface-controlled creep mechanism.

Failure to observe a statistically significant creep-rate reduction and associated microstructural stabilization in multilayers relative to monolithic controls would falsify the proposed interface mechanism.
